name: Madhyamaka
alt_names: Śūnyavāda / Śūnyatāvāda (name mostly used by others)
regions: South India (Andhra: Śrīparvata / Nāgārjunakoṇḍa in the tradition's accounts)
Valabhī / western India (Bhāviveka in some accounts)

tradition.text: founded by Nāgārjuna, prophesied (Laṅkāvatāra) to appear four hundred years after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa; Tibetan histories give him a life of six hundred years

scholarly.text: Nāgārjuna c. 150–250 CE; Indian Madhyamaka active until the 12th c. CE

transmissions_received.what: the Perfection of Wisdom sūtras' teaching that all dharmas are empty, unborn and like illusions
transmissions_received.evidence: MMK and its commentaries cite the Prajñāpāramitā, Akṣayamatinirdeśa, Anavataptanāgarājaparipṛcchā and Kāśyapaparivarta

transmissions_received.what: dependent origination as the middle between 'is' and 'is not'; the unanswered questions; no-self
transmissions_received.evidence: MMK 15.7 names the Kātyāyanāvavāda (= Kaccānagotta Sutta); MMK 11.1 and 27 rework āgama teachings

transmissions_given.what: the Middle Treatise, Twelve Gate Treatise and Hundred Treatise translated by Kumārajīva (Three-Treatise school)
MMK 24.18 read as the basis of the three truths (emptiness, provisional, middle)
Candrakīrti's Madhyamaka through Atiśa and the Kadam lineage
Prāsaṅgika-Madhyamaka as the final view in Tsongkhapa's system
Madhyamaka as the view of the sūtra path
Nāgārjuna named as the fourteenth Indian patriarch in Chan transmission lists (the tradition's account)
the 'easy path' chapter of the Daśabhūmikavibhāṣā attributed to Nāgārjuna; Nāgārjuna as the first of Shinran's seven patriarchs

distinctive_positions: Every dharma is empty (śūnya) of own-nature (svabhāva) because it arises in dependence; emptiness = dependent origination = dependent designation = the middle way (MMK 24.18).
Things do not arise from themselves, from another, from both, or without cause (MMK 1.1).

The Buddhas teach by relying on two truths, the worldly-conventional and the ultimate; without relying on the conventional the ultimate cannot be taught, and without reaching the ultimate nirvāṇa is not attained (MMK 24.8–10).
Emptiness is not a view: it is the relinquishing of all views, and those who make emptiness a view are called incurable (MMK 13.8).
The Mādhyamika has no thesis of his own to defend (VV 29) and refutes the opponent's positions on their own terms.
There is not the slightest difference between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa (MMK 25.19–20); nirvāṇa is neither existent nor nonexistent (25.4–10).
Emptiness is not nihilism: for one for whom emptiness is possible, everything — the four truths, karma, the path — is possible (MMK 24.14; VV 70).
The self is neither the same as nor different from the aggregates; it is a designation dependent on them (MMK 18.1; 27; MA 6).
The bodhisattva path unites wisdom (emptiness) and method (compassion, bodhicitta, the perfections) (RĀ; BCA; BhK).
summary: The Middle Way school founded by Nāgārjuna (c. 2nd c. CE) on the Perfection of Wisdom sūtras. It teaches that all things, including the Buddha, nirvāṇa and emptiness itself, lack own-nature because they arise dependently, and that this emptiness, rightly understood through the two truths, is the middle way between eternalism and annihilationism. Its Indian lines — the commentators on Nāgārjuna and Āryadeva (Buddhapālita, Bhāviveka, Candrakīrti), the bodhisattva manuals (Śāntideva) and the synthesis with Yogācāra and Buddhist logic (Śāntarakṣita, Kamalaśīla) — were classified by later Tibetan doxographers as Prāsaṅgika and Svātantrika; the school's view became the philosophical centre of Tibetan Buddhism and, as Sanlun, of East Asian Madhyamaka.

name: Prāsaṅgika-Madhyamaka

scholarly.text: Buddhapālita c. 470–540 CE; Candrakīrti c. 600–650 CE; the label 'Prāsaṅgika' (thal 'gyur ba) is a Tibetan doxographical category of the 11th–12th c., not a name Candrakīrti used

transmissions_received.what: Nāgārjuna's and Āryadeva's texts and method of refuting by consequences

transmissions_given.what: Prāsaṅgika as the highest view, as systematized by Tsongkhapa

distinctive_positions: The Mādhyamika need only draw out the unwanted consequences (prasaṅga) of the opponent's own theses; he does not use autonomous inferences (svatantra-anumāna) whose subject and reasons would have to be established for both parties by their own nature (Candrakīrti, Prasannapadā ch.1).
Nothing has own-nature even conventionally; the conventional is accepted only as the world accepts it (lokaprasiddhi).
Each thing bears two natures, the one found by correct seeing (the ultimate) and the one found by false seeing (the conventional) (MA 6.23).
Reflexive awareness (svasaṃvedana) and a storehouse consciousness are rejected even conventionally (MA 6; BCA 9.17–25).
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas also realize the selflessness of phenomena (Candrakīrti, MA bhāṣya on 1.8).
The ultimate is not within the domain of the intellect; the intellect is conventional (BCA 9.2).
summary: The line of Madhyamaka exegesis that follows Buddhapālita's commentary on the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā as defended by Candrakīrti against Bhāviveka's criticism: emptiness is shown by reducing the opponent's positions to absurd consequences, without autonomous proofs, and no own-nature is admitted at any level. Śāntideva, Prajñākaramati, Jayānanda and Atiśa are counted in it by Tibetan doxographers, for whom (from Patsab Nyima Drak onward) it became the highest Buddhist view.

name: Svātantrika-Madhyamaka
regions: India (Nālandā; Bhāviveka's seat given in some accounts as in the south)

scholarly.text: Bhāviveka c. 500–570 CE; Jñānagarbha 8th c.; the name 'Svātantrika' (rang rgyud pa) is a Tibetan doxographical category

transmissions_received.what: Dignāga's formal inference (the three-mode reason) applied to proving emptiness

transmissions_given.what: early Tibetan Madhyamaka (Ngok Loden Sherab's line) read Madhyamaka through Svātantrika authors

distinctive_positions: A Mādhyamika must be able to state an autonomous inference (svatantra-anumāna) with thesis, reason and example; Buddhapālita's bare consequences are faulty (Bhāviveka, Prajñāpradīpa ch.1).
Negations of arising and the like are qualified 'ultimately' (paramārthataḥ); conventionally things arise as they appear.
Conventional truth is divided into the correct conventional (tathya-saṃvṛti), capable of efficacy as it appears, and the incorrect (mithyā-saṃvṛti) (Jñānagarbha).
The ultimate is divided into the nominal or concordant ultimate (paryāya-paramārtha), the object of reasoning, and the non-nominal ultimate beyond elaboration (Bhāviveka).
Bhāviveka accepts external objects conventionally (hence 'Sautrāntika-Svātantrika' in Tibetan doxography) and criticizes Yogācāra, Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Vedānta and Mīmāṃsā in the Madhyamakahṛdaya.
summary: The line of Madhyamaka that, following Bhāviveka's criticism of Buddhapālita, holds that emptiness must be established by autonomous formal inferences in Dignāga's manner, qualifying its negations as 'ultimate', and that admits conventional arising as it appears. Tibetan doxographers divided it into the Sautrāntika-Svātantrika (Bhāviveka, Jñānagarbha, Śrīgupta) and the Yogācāra-Svātantrika (Śāntarakṣita, Kamalaśīla, Haribhadra). Its Indian authors did not use the name.

name: Yogācāra-Madhyamaka
alt_names: Yogācāra-Svātantrika-Madhyamaka (Tibetan doxography: rnal 'byor spyod pa'i dbu ma rang rgyud pa)
regions: Tibet (Samye; the first ordinations under Śāntarakṣita)

tradition.text: Śāntarakṣita was invited to Tibet by King Trisong Detsen and founded Samye with Padmasambhava; Kamalaśīla defended the gradual path at Samye

scholarly.text: 8th c. CE (Śāntarakṣita c. 725–788; Kamalaśīla c. 740–795) to the 11th c.

transmissions_received.what: mind-only (cittamātra) as the account of conventional reality

transmissions_given.what: Śāntarakṣita's and Kamalaśīla's teachings at Samye; later commented on by Mipham (Madhyamakālaṃkāra commentary)
the Bhāvanākrama's gradual path of calm and insight

distinctive_positions: Nothing that is held to be real by ourselves or others is truly one or truly many; therefore it lacks own-nature, like a reflection (MAL 1).

Conventionally all appearances are mind only; ultimately even mind is without own-nature — relying on mind-only one understands the absence of external things, relying on Madhyamaka one understands that even that mind lacks self (MAL 92–93).
Consciousness is by nature self-illuminating (svasaṃvedana) at the conventional level (MAL 16–17).
Riding the two chariots of Yogācāra and Madhyamaka and holding the reins of reasoning, one is a true Mahāyānist (MAL 93, the tradition's summary).
Meditation must be preceded by correct analysis (bhūtapratyavekṣā); mere non-thought is not non-conceptual wisdom (Bhāvanākrama III).
summary: The 8th-century synthesis in which Śāntarakṣita and Kamalaśīla combined Madhyamaka's emptiness (shown chiefly by the 'neither one nor many' argument), Yogācāra's mind-only as the description of conventional reality, and Dharmakīrti's epistemology; their encyclopaedic Tattvasaṅgraha and Pañjikā examine and reject the positions of every Indian school. Kamalaśīla's Bhāvanākramas set out the gradual path of compassion, bodhicitta, calm and insight. Tibetan doxography classifies the line as Yogācāra-Svātantrika, sub-divided into true-aspectarian and false-aspectarian branches.
notes: Parent set to lin:svatantrika following the Tibetan doxographical classification that the registry names follow; the Indian authors did not call themselves Svātantrika.
